note.explanation: A thermometer is judged by three features: sensitivity (detecting small temperature changes), range (the temperatures it measures), and linearity (equal temperature changes giving equal scale changes). For example, a thermometer marked every 0.1°C is more sensitive than one marked every 1°C. A clinical thermometer has a short range, while a laboratory thermometer can have a longer range. A linear thermometer has evenly spaced scale markings.
examples: A thermometer with 0.1°C divisions is more sensitive than one with 1°C divisions.
A thermometer with evenly spaced scale markings shows linearity.
note.checkAnswer: Sensitivity is the ability to detect small temperature changes.
note.simple: Sensitivity tells how small a change a thermometer can notice. Range tells how low and high a temperature it can measure. Linearity means equal temperature changes produce equal scale changes.
note.checkQuestion: What does sensitivity tell us about a thermometer?
note.title: Sensitivity, Range and Linearity
steps: Check the smallest scale division to compare sensitivity: smaller divisions allow smaller changes to be detected.
Find the lowest and highest temperatures marked to identify the range.
Check whether equal temperature changes correspond to equal scale intervals to identify linearity.
note.answer: Sensitivity is the ability to detect small temperature changes; range is the span of temperatures measured; linearity means equal temperature changes correspond to equal scale changes.

examTips: These ideas are commonly tested as short definitions and as a comprehensive question asking you to define sensitivity, range and linearity with examples.
For sensitivity, state that it detects small temperature changes; use the 0.1°C and 1°C divisions example if asked to explain.
For range, state that it is the span of temperatures measured accurately, then give the clinical thermometer range of about 35°C to 45°C or a laboratory range such as −10°C to 110°C.
For linearity, include both the proportional relationship and the idea that equal temperature changes correspond to equal scale changes.
When asked about thermometer design, name the design change and explain how it affects sensitivity, range or linearity.

explain.title: Sensitivity
explain.body: Sensitivity of a thermometer refers to its ability to detect small changes in the temperature of an object. For example, a thermometer marked every 0.1°C is more sensitive than one marked every 1°C.

explain.title: Range
explain.body: This refers to the span of temperature, from low to high, over which the thermometer can measure accurately. A clinical thermometer has a short range, about 35°C to 45°C, while a laboratory thermometer may have a longer range.

explain.title: The liquid affects range
explain.body: The choice of liquid for thermometers puts a lower and upper limit for the range of a thermometer. Mercury freezes at −39°C and boils at 357°C; alcohol freezes at about −112°C and boils at 78°C.

explain.title: Linearity
explain.body: This refers to a direct proportional relationship between the temperature and scale reading across entire range of measurement. A good linear thermometer has evenly spaced markings, so equal scale increments correspond to equal temperature changes.

mistakes: Do not confuse sensitivity with range: sensitivity is about detecting small changes, while range is the span of temperatures measured.
Do not define linearity only as having evenly spaced marks; explain that equal temperature changes correspond to equal scale changes.
Do not say that a narrow range makes a thermometer more sensitive; these are different properties.
When comparing scale divisions, remember that smaller divisions indicate greater sensitivity.
Give the correct example for each property: small divisions for sensitivity, low-to-high temperature span for range, and equal increments for linearity.
